entries.note: Named after [[Latium]], the ancient region around Rome and the lower Tiber, now called Lazio; Latinus meant 'of Latium' and also named the language.
Borrowed from Old French, from a late Latin sense of 'in the Roman manner'; it gave Romance languages and romances for novels that celebrated the classics.
Germanic dialects took it from the Romans on the continent, before English existed in Britain.
Like [[wine]], a Latin word taken from the Romans by Germanic speakers before English existed.
An early Latin borrowing from mille passus, because a Roman mile was a thousand paces long.
Taken from Latin on the continent, originally in a battle sense; related to German Kampf and to the later French borrowings [[campaign]] and [[champion]].
From Latin strata, as in [[via]] strata, a straight road, so saying street is essentially saying 'straight'.
From Latin vallum, which in classical Latin was pronounced with a W sound.
From Latin castellum, a fort or stronghold, which entered late Old English through biblical usage; it was later borrowed again from French as château.
From Latin altare, a Christian-era borrowing; it's thought to come from [[adolere]], 'to burn', rather than altus, 'high', because offerings were burned there.
From Latin scrinium, a chest; it came to mean a chest holding a saint's relic, then a venerated place itself.
Ultimately from Latin pulvinus, a little cushion or small pillow, possibly reaching other Germanic languages first.
Jess's favourite root, meaning way, road, path, channel or course, hidden in [[obvious]], [[impervious]], [[trivia]], [[voyage]] and [[invoice]].
One of the words Jess used with fifth graders to teach a Latin root meaning 'to talk', along with [[loquacious]] and [[soliloquy]].
The pupils guessed it from [[eloquent]] and [[soliloquy]], which share its root meaning 'to talk or speak'.
Some pupils already knew it; it shares the root meaning 'to talk' with [[eloquent]] and [[grandiloquent]].
Grand ('big') plus the root meaning 'to talk', so literally 'big talking'; William Barnes proposed [[high-talking]] in its place.
Sleep-talking; the pupils worked it out from [[insomnia]] and the talk root in [[grandiloquent]].
Literally 'in the way', in front of you on the road, from [[via]]: so plain you might trip over it.
Im- 'not', per 'through' and [[via]] 'road': something with no way through, and so resistant to attack.
Something that occurs earlier on your route or path, from [[via]].
To stray away from the course, from [[via]].
Being devious or deviant means straying from the moral path, from [[via]].
From viaticum, 'a journey', related to [[via]], with French influence along the way.
To carry something with you along a road, from [[via]].
Someone sent somewhere to represent someone else; from [[via]] and related to [[invoice]].
Related to [[envoy]]: a request for payment to be sent along. There's no voice in it, but there is a road ([[via]]).
Literally 'three roads', a Roman crossroads where people met and swapped news; the fun-fact sense comes from Logan Pearsall Smith's 1902 book series Trivia.
Refers to the inconsequential talk of commoners at Roman crossroads, the [[trivia]].
Classical education's three arts of grammar, logic and rhetoric, named during the Carolingian Renaissance; they came before the [[quadrivium]] and underlie today's liberal arts.
The more advanced studies that followed the [[trivium]]: arithmetic, astronomy, music and geometry.
Latin 'to hang'; Jess strings fourteen descendants together, including expend, compendium, depend, pendulum, suspense, [[ponder]] and [[pensive]].
From pensare, 'to weigh or consider', a frequentative of [[pendere]]: something hanging on your mind.
From Latin ponderare, 'to weigh', from [[pendere]]; Rob suggests it's spelled the way a French speaker would say it.
From libra pondo, with pondo meaning weight, which Rob ties to [[ponder]]: weighty, hanging things.
Latin 'to hold', found in [[maintain]], abstain, entertain, obtain and detain.
Literally 'to hold in the hand', from [[tenere]]; an example of how literal Latin compounds really are.
Name of the backlash against classical borrowings during the Renaissance; perhaps because long Latinate words meant dipping your quill into an inkhorn again and again.
Sir John Cheke's native replacement for centurion in his Gospel of Matthew, written to avoid excessive borrowings in the [[inkhorn]] spirit.
Cheke's substitute for crucified, which Jess says sounds like a euphemism.
Cheke's native term in his Matthew for the removal to Babylon; the hosts compare it to diaspora or Exodus and note that it isn't any shorter.
William Barnes's Germanic alternative to astronomy.
William Barnes's Germanic alternative to ornithology, alongside [[starlore]].
William Barnes's Germanic replacement for [[grandiloquent]].
A purist coinage used for [[logic]], not knowledge, since know is already Germanic; it fits the original sense of wit, and reason and idea were ruled out as French.
An example of assimilation: sub- plus a root meaning 'to look', so being under observation.
sub- assimilated before cedere to mean 'come after'.
sub- plus ferre, 'to carry', so to be under a burden; another example of assimilation.
Latin prefix meaning not, away or broadly, as in distribute; French words beginning de- or des- carry the same prefix after it passed through French.
One of many ob- words, from oblivio, 'forgetfulness'; sending something into oblivion means wiping it away into empty nothingness.
Ob- plus litera: to erase or blot out writing, an idea close to [[oblivion]].
Toward noxa, 'hurt or injury'; the Latin predecessor meant injurious, much stronger than today's 'annoying'.
Covered in the magic episode; its initial o- is an assimilated ob-.
Ob-, here 'in front of or before', plus fuscare, 'to make dark'.
Ob- plus scurus, 'covered', the same element as in [[chiaroscuro]].
From the art episode; meaning 'bright dark', it shares its dark element with [[obscure]].
A little-known ob- word meaning walking around; it reminds Rob of [[somnambulation]].
Sleepwalking; the word Rob was reaching for after [[obambulation]].
A Latin suffix English happily adds to Germanic stems (watchable, winnable, knowable), making hybrids alongside Romance words like visible and portable.
A hybrid of Latin inter and Greek planet; avoiding such hybrids produced [[intermundane]].
An 18th-century non-hybrid alternative to [[interplanetary]], with mundane meaning worldly.
From a recent episode: octopodes follows Greek, but the word didn't exist in Greek, and octopi isn't the Latin plural either, so octopuses is best.
Its Latin plural is prospectus, not prospecti, so English uses prospectuses; it shows that -us doesn't always become -i.
Its Latin plural is status, not stati; English says statuses.
Its Latin plural is apparatus, not apparati; some circles still use apparatus as the plural, while apparatuses sounds odd.
Latin for 'body', whose plural is corpora, not corpi.
Latin for 'hand', whose plural is also manus, not mani.
The singular of algae; English has no native plural such as algas, and algae is also used as a singular.
A Latin plural of agendum used as a singular; from agere, 'to do', originally a theological term paired with [[credenda]].
A theological counterpart to [[agenda]]: things to be believed alongside things to be done.
Discussed in an earlier episode: agent, act and [[actor]] share the Latin root of [[agenda]]; actors and agents are both doers.
In Latin a doorkeeper or porter, related to [[Janus]], the two-faced god of doorways; it later meant a school usher, then a caretaker by the 1700s.
Named after [[Janus]], the god related to [[janitor]].
Originally a sandy place, since Roman amphitheatres were strewn with sand to soak up blood; the exact root is unknown and may be Etruscan.
From medieval Latin dies mali, the two unlucky days each month, also called [[Egyptian days]]; first used in 'in the dismal', then the tautological 'dismal day'.
Another name for the dies mali behind [[dismal]], supposedly calculated by ancient Egyptian scholars or linked to the story of the plagues.
Roman calendar lists of official and religious events and of dies fasti, days allowed for business; Jess enjoys that the source is 'the fasti of Furius'.
Originally 'lasting one day', from [[dies]]; a doublet of [[journal]], covered in a previous episode.
The word diurnal squeezed through French; a doublet of [[diary]].
Originally noon or midday ('night's meridian' meant midnight); from [[dies]], Latin medidies became meridies by dissimilation.
